questions.q: You're partway through a GDB session with many breakpoints set, and you've just fixed a bug in the C source. What's the most convenient way to rebuild the program and keep debugging?
choices: Quit GDB, run `make` in the shell, restart GDB, and set the breakpoints again
Use `attach` to connect GDB to the newly compiled executable
questions.explain: GDB accepts the `make` command. If the build succeeds, the next `run` starts the newly built program, and all your breakpoints are still set.

questions.q: If you add or delete source lines and then rebuild with `make` from inside GDB, your existing breakpoints are guaranteed to stay at the same logical place in the new program.
questions.explain: Adding or removing lines can shift code, so an old breakpoint may no longer be at the same logical spot in the new version.

questions.q: After rebuilding with `make` inside GDB, your old breakpoints no longer point at the right code because lines were added. Which of these are reasonable fixes?
choices: Exit GDB and start a new GDB session on the new executable
Use `delete` to remove the old breakpoints, then `break` to set new ones
Use `disable` to turn off the old breakpoints, then `break` to set new ones
Do nothing, because GDB automatically moves breakpoints to match the edited source
questions.explain: Either restart GDB on the new executable, or disable/delete the old breakpoints and set new ones with `break`. GDB does not move breakpoints to match edited source.

questions.q: Which shell command lists all processes and keeps only the ones named a.out, so you can find the PID to attach GDB to?
questions.explain: `ps -A` lists all processes, and piping it through `grep a.out` keeps only the a.out processes along with their PIDs.

questions.q: An executable named a.out is already running as PID 12345. Which commands start GDB attached to that process?
questions.explain: The two forms are `gdb <executable> <pid>` and `gdb attach <pid> <executable>`.

questions.q: When GDB attaches to a running process, it pauses that process so you can enter GDB commands before execution continues.
questions.explain: Attaching pauses the process. You can then enter GDB commands before letting it continue.

questions.q: Complete this C call, which makes a program pause itself so a debugger can be attached: kill(getpid(), ______)
questions.explain: `kill(getpid(), SIGSTOP)` sends a SIGSTOP signal to the calling process, which stops it until you attach GDB to it.

questions.q: You've attached GDB to a paused process, but `cont` doesn't get it running again. Which GDB command explicitly makes the process resume?
questions.explain: `signal SIGCONT` sends the process a continue signal so it resumes running. SIGSTOP would pause it instead.

questions.q: By default, which process does GDB follow after the debugged program calls fork()?
choices: Both processes at the same time
Neither; GDB detaches at the fork
questions.explain: GDB follows the parent by default. The process GDB isn't following runs without being affected by GDB.

questions.q: Write the full GDB command that makes GDB follow the child process after a fork().
questions.explain: `set follow-fork-mode child` switches to the child, `set follow-fork-mode parent` switches back, and `show follow-fork-mode` shows the current setting.

questions.q: Which GDB command shows whether GDB is currently set to follow the parent or the child on a fork?
questions.explain: `show follow-fork-mode` shows the current setting, and `set follow-fork-mode` changes it.

questions.q: How can you debug both the parent and the child after a fork(), using one GDB session per process?
choices: Let the first GDB follow the parent, have the child send itself SIGSTOP right after the fork, then attach a second GDB to the child
Put a breakpoint on fork() and GDB automatically opens a second session for the child
Have the parent send itself SIGBUS so GDB switches to the child
questions.explain: GDB follows the parent while the child pauses itself with SIGSTOP. That gives you time to attach a second GDB to the child before it continues.

questions.q: Setting breakpoints at fork() calls is useful when you want to change which process GDB follows during a session.
questions.explain: Stopping at a fork() call lets you change follow-fork-mode before the fork happens.

questions.q: A program tries to access memory using an address that is misaligned for the type being accessed. Which signal does it usually receive?
questions.explain: A misaligned memory access usually triggers SIGBUS, and the process usually exits.

questions.q: By default, GDB lets the process exit when it gets a SIGBUS. Write the GDB command that makes GDB stop and take control instead, so you can look at the program's state.
questions.explain: `handle SIGBUS stop` changes how GDB handles SIGBUS, so GDB takes control when the program receives it.

questions.q: Which statements about GDB signal commands are correct?
choices: `signal <SIG>` sends a signal to the process being debugged
`handle <SIG> stop` makes GDB take control when the process receives that signal
`info signal` lists how GDB handles every signal
`signal <SIG>` only changes how GDB reacts to a signal and never sends one
questions.explain: `signal` sends a signal, `handle` sets how GDB responds to signals the process receives, and `info` shows how GDB handles signals (all of them, or one, as in `info SIGALRM`).

questions.q: Which GDB command shows how GDB handles just the SIGALRM signal?
questions.explain: `info SIGALRM` shows how GDB handles that one signal. `signal SIGALRM` would actually send it to the process.

questions.q: Where does DDD save settings such as subwindow sizes and whether the register and assembly windows are shown?
choices: In a .ddd directory in your home directory
In a .gdbinit file in the current directory
Nowhere; DDD starts with default settings every time
questions.explain: DDD keeps its settings in ~/.ddd so you don't have to set your preferences again every time you start it.

questions.q: If DDD hangs at startup showing "Waiting until GDB ready", a common fix is to delete the ~/.ddd directory, which also erases all your saved DDD settings.
questions.explain: This hang often comes from an error in the saved settings files. Running `rm -rf ~/.ddd` fixes it, but you'll have to set your preferences again.
